market_context: United States and general English-speaking market
title: What does the cacao percentage on chocolate mean?

seo.title: What does cacao percentage on chocolate mean?
seo.meta_description: A 70% bar is not 70% cocoa powder. Learn what the percentage includes, what fills the rest of the recipe, and what it cannot tell you about flavanols or calories.
seo.search_intent: Understand what a chocolate bar's cacao percentage represents

excerpt: Cacao percentage is the total share of cacao-derived ingredients in the bar: chocolate liquor/cocoa mass, cocoa butter, and sometimes cocoa powder. A 70% bar is not 70% cocoa powder or 70% nonfat solids; the remaining 30% is sugar and any other non-cacao ingredients.
content_html:
“70% cacao” sounds precise because it is precise about one thing: how much of the bar comes from cacao-derived ingredients. It does not tell you how much of that is cocoa butter, how much is nonfat cocoa solids, or how many flavanols are present.

What counts toward the 70%

The cacao share can include chocolate liquor or cocoa mass—which already contains both cocoa solids and cocoa butter—plus added cocoa butter and, in some recipes, cocoa powder.

If a 100 g bar is labeled 70% cacao, about 70 g of the recipe comes from those cacao ingredients. The remaining 30 g can be sugar plus small amounts of vanilla or emulsifier, or other non-cacao ingredients in a more elaborate bar.

It does not mean 70% cocoa powder

This is the most common misunderstanding. Cocoa powder is only one possible cacao ingredient. Chocolate needs fat for its characteristic melt, so a meaningful share of the percentage can come from cocoa butter already present in cocoa mass or added separately.

That means two 70% bars can have different fat, fiber, and texture while showing the same number on the front.

What usually happens to sugar as the number rises

In a simple dark chocolate, a higher cacao percentage leaves less room for sugar. A 70% recipe has at most 30% of its weight available for all non-cacao ingredients; an 85% bar leaves 15%; a 100% bar leaves none.

That makes percentage a useful clue about sweetness, but not an exact sugar calculator. Nuts, fruit, milk ingredients, emulsifiers, or non-sugar sweeteners can also occupy the remainder.

What the number cannot tell you

  • It does not give grams of flavanols.
  • It does not separate cocoa butter from nonfat cocoa solids.
  • It does not guarantee a certain amount of fiber, iron, or magnesium.
  • It does not reveal whether cocoa was alkalized.
  • It does not predict calories without the Nutrition Facts panel.

An 85% bar can even be more calorie-dense than a 70% bar if it contains more cocoa butter, despite having much less sugar.

Is 100% cacao simply ground cocoa beans?

Not necessarily in a single form. A 100% bar can combine cocoa mass, cocoa butter, and cocoa powder, as long as the recipe is entirely cacao-derived. A current Lindt U.S. 100% bar, for example, lists chocolate, alkalized cocoa powder, and cocoa butter.

How to read a bar quickly

Use the percentage to understand how cacao-heavy the recipe is. Then read the ingredient list to see which cacao forms are used and what fills the remainder. Finally check sugar and fat per equal serving weight if nutrition is your goal.

Cacao percentage is a recipe proportion, not a quality grade and not a health score.

faq.question: What does 70% cacao mean?
faq.answer: Roughly 70% of the bar's weight comes from cacao-derived ingredients such as chocolate liquor/cocoa mass, cocoa butter, and cocoa powder.

faq.question: Does a 70% bar contain 30% sugar?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. The remaining 30% includes everything that is not cacao, which may include sugar, vanilla, emulsifiers, nuts, or other ingredients.

faq.question: Does 100% cacao have added sugar?
faq.answer: A true 100% cacao bar has no room for non-cacao ingredients such as added sugar, though tiny amounts of naturally occurring sugars can still be present.

faq.question: Does a higher cacao percentage mean more flavanols?
faq.answer: Not reliably. The percentage includes cocoa butter and does not reveal processing history, both of which limit what can be inferred about flavanols.
